nameStory: The cecropia moth gets its name from Cecropia, the mythical first king of Athens in Greek mythology. Carl Linnaeus, who first scientifically described this species in 1758, chose this regal name fitting for North America's largest native moth. The name suggests the grandeur and majesty of this impressive giant silk moth.
description: The cecropia moth is North America's largest native moth and truly lives up to its royal name. These magnificent insects belong to the giant silk moth family and can have wingspans reaching five to seven inches or more in females. Their wings display beautiful patterns of reddish-brown, white, and black with distinctive eye-spots and crescent-shaped markings. As adults, they're fuzzy, robust moths with feathery antennae that give them an almost mythical appearance.

idTips.label: Massive wingspan
idTips.description: Enormous size sets them apart immediately - females can span 5-7 inches across, larger than many small birds, with wings that feel surprisingly delicate despite their impressive scale

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Rich reddish-brown wings with white crescents and prominent eye-spots that look like they're watching you, bordered by bands of black and white

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Males have especially elaborate, feathery antennae that feel soft and delicate to the touch, like tiny fern fronds designed to detect female pheromones from miles away

idTips.label: Fuzzy body
idTips.description: Thick, robust body covered in dense, soft fur-like scales that feel like velvet when gently touched, much fluffier than typical moths

idTips.label: Red and white crescents
idTips.description: Distinctive crescent-shaped markings in bright white and red create an almost stained-glass window effect on each wing

idTips.label: No feeding parts
idTips.description: Adults have no functional mouthparts and cannot eat - they live entirely off fat reserves stored during their caterpillar stage

habitat: Cecropia moths are found throughout New England wherever their host trees grow, particularly in areas with maple, cherry, and birch trees. They prefer forest edges, suburban areas with mature trees, parks, and anywhere deciduous trees provide food for their caterpillars. Adults are most commonly spotted near outdoor lights at night during their brief flying season.

seasonality.spring: Large green caterpillars with colorful tubercles can be found munching on maple, cherry, and birch leaves, growing rapidly as they prepare for pupation.
seasonality.summer: Adults emerge in late spring to early summer for their brief but spectacular mating flight, lasting only about two weeks as they cannot feed.
seasonality.fall: Tough, brown cocoons become visible on bare branches after leaves drop, securely attached and weatherproofing for winter survival.
seasonality.winter: Pupae remain dormant inside their silk cocoons, enduring New England's harsh winters while transforming from caterpillar to moth.

funFact: Adult cecropia moths have no mouth or stomach and cannot eat anything at all - they live their entire adult lives, which last only about two weeks, burning through the fat reserves they stored up as caterpillars, making their brief existence entirely devoted to finding a mate and reproducing.
confusionNotes: Cecropia moths are sometimes confused with other large silk moths like the polyphemus or promethea moths, but cecropias are significantly larger and have distinctive white crescent markings. Remember: "Cecropia's crescents" - the white crescent shapes are the giveaway feature that separates them from other giant moths.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "giant silk moths," cecropia cocoons were never used commercially for silk production like those of domestic silkworms. The silk is too coarse and the cocoons too difficult to unravel, though Native Americans did sometimes use the strong cocoon fibers for fishing line and other purposes.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus found in New England, cecropia moths are best compared to other members of the giant silk moth family. They're significantly larger than polyphemus moths and lack the long tails of luna moths. Unlike promethea moths, cecropias have much more prominent white crescent markings and lack the distinct pink and yellow coloration of fresh prometheas.
